titleEn: Save me, God, the waters have reached my neck
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Thirty seven verses: thirty of drowning, seven of singing. It opens with water at the throat and mud with no floor under it, spends twenty verses on shame inflicted by other people rather than by an army, curses those people for seven verses, and ends with Zion rebuilt and lived in. This is a lament of the individual, the kind of psalm said when the trouble is other people. For a learner it is a workshop of the object suffix: save me, answer me, rescue me, sweep me away, swallow me, ransom me, redeem it, all one syllable hung on the end of a verb.

stichs.en: For the leader; upon shoshannim.
Of David.

verses.summary: The heading gives a tune and an author and says nothing about the contents. Shoshannim, lilies, is a musical direction whose tune is lost.

stichs.en: Save me, God,
for the waters have come up to my neck.

verses.summary: The psalm starts at the end of the crisis, not the beginning of it. The water is already at the throat, and everything that follows is the argument for the imperative in the first word.

stichs.en: I have sunk in deep mire, and there is no foothold;
I have come into deep waters, and the current has swept me away.

verses.summary: Two pairs, mud then water, and each pair carries a clause saying there is nothing to stand on. The verbs are perfect: this has already happened to him.

stichs.en: I am worn out by my calling; my throat is parched.
My eyes have failed, waiting for my God.

verses.summary: The exhaustion comes from praying, not from fighting. The throat that has been shouting is the same throat the water reached in the verse before.

stichs.en: More than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause;
many are those who would destroy me, my enemies with lies.
What I never stole, I am made to give back.

verses.summary: The count moves off the water and onto people. Hairs of the head is the standard image for a number past counting, and the last clause is a courtroom formula: he is made to repay what he never took.

stichs.en: God, You Yourself know my folly,
and my guilty acts are not hidden from You.

verses.summary: A break in the protest. He does not claim to be innocent in general, only that whatever the guilt is, God already holds the full account of it.

stichs.en: Let those who hope in You not be shamed through me, my Lord GOD of hosts;
let those who seek You not be disgraced through me, God of Israel.

verses.summary: The stakes widen past one man. If he is shamed, everyone who hopes in the same God is shamed with him, which makes his rescue their business too.

stichs.en: For it is for Your sake that I have borne reproach,
that disgrace has covered my face.

verses.summary: Here is the reason for the reproach: it was incurred on God's account. This is the hinge that turns a private complaint into a claim with a case behind it.

stichs.en: I have become a stranger to my brothers,
a foreigner to my mother's sons.

verses.summary: The isolation reaches the family. My mother's sons is the tighter of the two idioms in a household with more than one wife, so the estrangement here is complete.

stichs.en: For zeal for Your house has consumed me,
and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me.

verses.summary: The most quoted line in the psalm. Zeal for the house eats the one who has it, and insults aimed at God land on whoever is standing nearest to it.

stichs.en: I wept, my soul in fasting,
and that became a reproach against me.

verses.summary: Public mourning gets read by the onlookers as one more thing to mock. The fast was meant as an appeal and turns into evidence against him.

stichs.en: I made sackcloth my clothing,
and I became a byword to them.

verses.summary: Sackcloth is the visible half of the fast in the previous verse. A byword is a person turned into a proverb: quoted rather than heard.

stichs.en: Those who sit at the gate talk about me,
and I am the song of the drinkers.

verses.summary: Two audiences, top and bottom: the elders at the gate where cases are judged, and the men drinking. Both have him for material.

stichs.en: But as for me, my prayer is to You, LORD, at a time of favour.
God, in Your abundant kindness, answer me with the truth of Your deliverance.

verses.summary: The turn. After twelve verses of description comes the first request since verse 2, and it is framed by timing: a moment of favour, when the appeal will be received.

stichs.en: Rescue me from the mud, and let me not sink;
let me be delivered from those who hate me, and out of deep water.

verses.summary: The water and mud of verses 2 and 3 come back, now as petitions. What was reported as accomplished fact is what he asks not to be finished.

stichs.en: Let no flood of water sweep me away,
let the deep not swallow me,
and let the pit not shut its mouth over me.

verses.summary: Three prohibitions, each with a different mouth: the flood, the deep that swallows, and the pit that closes. The pit shutting is burial.

stichs.en: Answer me, LORD, for Your kindness is good;
in Your abundant mercy, turn to me.

verses.summary: The ground of the request is not his own merit but the quality of the kindness he is asking from. Answer me, the same imperative, returns from verse 14.

stichs.en: Do not hide Your face from Your servant,
for I am in distress; answer me quickly.

verses.summary: A hidden face is the standard image for attention withheld. The new element in the request is speed, which is what distress does to prayer.

stichs.en: Draw near to my soul, redeem it;
because of my enemies, ransom me.

verses.summary: Two commercial verbs, redeem and ransom, both about paying to get a person back out of someone else's hands. What is being bought out is the soul.

stichs.en: You know my reproach, my shame and my disgrace;
all my adversaries are before You.

verses.summary: He goes back to what God knows, as in verse 6, but the object has changed. There it was his own folly; here it is the shame other people put on him.

stichs.en: Reproach has broken my heart and I am sick;
I hoped for sympathy, and there was none,
for comforters, and I found none.

verses.summary: The lowest point of the psalm, and it is not the enemies. It is the absence of anyone kind: he looked for a comforter and the looking itself came back empty.

stichs.en: They put poison in my food,
and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.

verses.summary: Hospitality turned into a weapon. Poison in the food and vinegar for the thirst are both handed over at exactly the moment of need.

stichs.en: Let their table before them become a snare,
and for those at ease, a trap.

verses.summary: The curses begin, and the first one sends the meal of verse 22 back to the sender. Their own table is what closes on them.

stichs.en: Let their eyes grow dark so they cannot see,
and make their loins tremble continually.

verses.summary: Darkened eyes and shaking hips: the two standard images for a body that can neither see what is coming nor run from it.

stichs.en: Pour out Your fury on them,
and let Your burning anger overtake them.

verses.summary: The one curse that asks God to act directly. The others ask for a state of affairs; this one asks for the pouring, with an imperative.

stichs.en: Let their camp be desolate,
let no one dwell in their tents.

verses.summary: Encampment and tents are the vocabulary of a household living in the open. The curse is that the line stops and the site stays empty.

stichs.en: For they pursue the one You have struck,
and they tell of the pain of those You have wounded.

verses.summary: The justification offered for the curses, and the hardest verse in the psalm to construe word by word. The charge is that they pile onto someone already struck down.

stichs.en: Add guilt to their guilt,
and let them not enter into Your righteousness.

verses.summary: Not a request for punishment but for the guilt itself to keep accumulating, since that is the one thing that would keep them outside.

stichs.en: Let them be erased from the book of the living,
and not be written down with the righteous.

verses.summary: The book of the living is a register of who is alive now. To be erased from it is to die, which is a smaller and harsher thing than being damned.

stichs.en: But I am afflicted and in pain;
let Your salvation, God, set me on high.

glosses: let it set me on high
verses.summary: The curses stop as abruptly as they started and the speaker goes back to his own state. Still poor, still in pain, and the verb asks to be lifted out of reach.

stichs.en: I will praise the name of God with a song,
and magnify Him with thanksgiving.

verses.summary: The vow of praise, which is where laments in this book normally land. Both nouns here, song and thanksgiving, also name things brought to the Temple.

stichs.en: And it will please the LORD more than an ox,
more than a bull with horns and hooves.

verses.summary: A ranking, stated flatly: the song is worth more than the animal. Horns and hooves are how you certify that the bull is fully grown and fit to bring.

stichs.en: The humble have seen it and rejoice;
you who seek God, let your heart revive.

verses.summary: The private rescue becomes public evidence. The humble who watch it are the audience the vow of verse 31 was made for.

stichs.en: For the LORD listens to the needy,
and He has not despised His prisoners.

verses.summary: The reason the humble can be glad, put as a rule about God rather than as a report about one rescued man.

stichs.en: Let heaven and earth praise Him,
the seas and everything that moves in them.

verses.summary: The audience widens to everything that exists, which is the standard closing move of a psalm of praise once the vow has been made.

stichs.en: For God will save Zion and build the cities of Judah,
and they will settle there and take possession of it.

verses.summary: The ending turns national. What opened with one man in the mud closes with cities rebuilt and a territory held, and the rescue asked for is now collective.

stichs.en: The offspring of His servants will inherit it,
and those who love His name will dwell in it.

verses.summary: The possession passes to a generation the speaker will not live to see. The last word of the psalm is a place, and the last verb is living in it.

pardes.body: Three movements. Verses 2 to 14 set out the trouble and give its cause: the speaker is drowning, and the reason people despise him is that he is identified with God's house. Verses 15 to 29 are the petition, first for rescue in the same water images that opened the psalm, then seven verses of curse against the people who did this. Verses 30 to 37 are the vow of praise and its widening, from the singer to the humble who watch, then heaven and earth, then Zion and the cities of Judah. Read as one argument it holds together: the rescue is asked for on the ground stated in {{8.1}}, that the reproach was incurred for God's sake, and the curses are justified in verse 27 on the ground that the enemies are attacking a man God has already wounded.

Three cruxes worth knowing. {{2.6}} is usually rendered soul, but the concrete sense of the word is throat, and with the water rising it is hard to read it any other way here. {{1.2}}, lilies, is a direction in the heading whose meaning is lost: it is taken as the name of a melody, as an instrument, or as a musical term nobody can now recover. And {{23.4}}, given above as those at ease, is genuinely disputed, read as their well being, as their allies, or as a state of security, with some editors changing the consonants to get a smoother sense. Outside the synagogue this psalm carries unusual weight: verses 10, 22 and 26 all reappear in the Christian scriptures, which is why it turns up in polemical literature far more than its neighbours in the book.

The curse section is why this psalm is hard to say out loud. Seven verses asking for blindness, desolation and erasure, and the tradition has never smoothed them over. One line of reading takes them as description rather than wish: this is what happens to people who kick a man who is already down, and the speaker is stating the consequence rather than calling it in. Another takes the whole psalm as spoken by the community in exile rather than by one man, which is the natural reading of the last two verses, where what is finally asked for is the rebuilding of the cities of Judah. On {{32.4}}, one classical reading notices that the word for horned is singular in form and identifies the animal with the ox that Adam offered, a single horn on its forehead, an animal older than the sacrificial system and therefore outside it. Either way the point is the ranking: what this psalm ends up offering is a song, not a bull.

The descent here is measured rather than chaotic: water closing over the head, then mud with no floor under it, then a body emptied by fasting, then a throat that can do nothing but sing. In the mystical reading that shape is the whole teaching. The return is not a reversal, because nothing that happened gets undone: the enemies of verse 5 are never removed, the cities of verse 36 are built anyway. The image the tradition works hardest is {{29.1}}, the book of the living, a register in which names are written and out of which they can be struck. The same phrase, a book of life, comes back in the insertions said during the Ten Days of Repentance. In this verse it is not about the world to come. It is about being counted among those who are still here.
